title: Celsus’s heap of misheard phrases
source_text: Μετὰ δὲ τὸ ἐκθέσθαι τὰ προειρημένα καὶ τὰ ἀνάλογον αὐτοῖς. ἅτινα ἡμεῖς προσεθήκαμεν, τοιαῦτά φησιν ὁ Κέλσος· οἱ δ᾿ ἔτι προστιθέασιν ἄλλα ἐπ᾿ ἄλλοις, προφητῶν λόγους καὶ κύκλους ἐπὶ κύκλοις καὶ ἀποῤῥοίας ἐκκλησίας ἐπιγείου καὶ περιτομῆς καὶ Προυνικοῦ τινος ῥέουσαν δύναμιν παρθένου καὶ ψυχὴν ζῶσαν καὶ σφαζόμενον οὐρανὸν, ἵνα ζήσῃ, καὶ γῆν σφαζομένην μαχαίρᾳ καὶ πολλοὺς σφαζομένους. ἵνα ζήσωσι, καὶ παυόμενον ἐν κόσμῳ θάνατον, ὅταν ἀποθάνῃ ἡ τοῦ κόσμου ἁμαρτία, καὶ κάθοδον αὖθις στενὴν καὶ αὐτομάτως ἀνοιγομένας πύλας· πανταχοῦ δὲ ἐκεῖ τὸ τῆς ζωῆς ξύλον καὶ ἀνάστασιν σαρκὸς ἀπὸ ξύλου, διότι οἶμαι ὁ διδάσκαλος αὐτῶν σταυρῷ ἐνηλώθη καὶ ἦν τέκτων τὴν τέχνην. ὡς εἰ ἔτυχεν ἐκεῖνος ἀπὸ κρημνοῦ ἐῤῥιμμένος ἢ εἰς βάραθρον ἐωσμένος ἢ ἀγχόνῃ πεπνιγμένος ἢ σκυτοτόμος ἢ λιθοξόος ἢ σιδηρεὺς. ἦν ἂν ὑπὲρ τοὺς οὐρανοὺς κρημνὸς ζωῆς ἢ βάραθρον ἀνα- στάσεως ἢ σχοινίον ἀθανασίας ἢ λίθος μακάριος ἢ σίδηρος ἀγάπης ἢ σκῦτος ἅγιόν [ἐστιν]. ἢ τίς γραῦς, ἐπὶ τῷ βαυκαλῆσαι παιδίον μῦθον ἐπᾴδουσα, τοιαῦτα ψιθυρίζειν οὐκ ἂν ᾐσχύνθη; ἐν τούτοις δὲ δοκεῖ μοι φύρειν τὰ παρακούσματα ὁ Κέλσος. εἰκὸς γὰρ ὅτι, εἴ τι ἤκουσεν οἱασδηποτοῦν αἱρέσεως λεξείδιον, μὴ τρανώσας αὐτὸ κἂν κατὰ τὸ βούλημα ἐκείνης ἀλλὰ τὰ ῥημάτια συμφορήσας, ἐπεδείκνυτο ἐν τοῖς μηδὲν ἐπισταμένοις μήτε τῶν ἡμετέρων μήτε τῶν ἐν ταῖς αἱρέσεσιν ὡς ἄρα πάντα τὰ Χριστιανῶν γινώσκοι. τοῦτο δὲ δῆλον ποιεῖ καὶ ἡ προκειμένη λέξις.
pass_a_gloss: After setting out the things said before and those analogous (ἀνάλογον) to them, which we have added (προσεθήκαμεν), Celsus says such things: 'They still add (προστιθέασιν) other things upon others: words of prophets (προφητῶν λόγους), circles upon circles, emanations (ἀπορροίας) of an earthly church and of circumcision (περιτομῆς), a flowing power (ῥέουσαν δύναμιν) of a certain virgin Prunicus (Προυνικοῦ), a living soul (ψυχὴν ζῶσαν), a heaven slaughtered (σφαζόμενον) that it may live, an earth slaughtered with a sword (μαχαίρᾳ), many slaughtered that they may live, death ceasing (παυόμενον) in the world when the sin of the world dies, again a narrow descent (κάθοδον στενήν), gates opening automatically; everywhere there the tree of life (τὸ τῆς ζωῆς ξύλον) and resurrection of flesh from a tree, because, I think, their teacher was nailed (ἐνηλώθη) to a cross (σταυρῷ) and was a carpenter (τέκτων) by craft. As if he had chanced to be thrown from a cliff (κρημνοῦ), or thrust into a pit (βάραθρον), or choked by a noose (ἀγχόνῃ), or been a shoemaker (σκυτοτόμος), stonecutter (λιθοξόος), or smith (σιδηρεύς), there would be above the heavens a cliff of life, a pit of resurrection, a rope of immortality (σχοινίον ἀθανασίας), a blessed stone, iron of love (σίδηρος ἀγάπης), holy leather (σκῦτος ἅγιον). Or what old woman (γραῦς), chanting a tale to lull (βαυκαλῆσαι) a child, would not be ashamed to whisper such things?' In these Celsus seems to me to mix (φύρειν) things misheard (παρακούσματα). For it is likely that, if he heard a little phrase (λεξείδιον) of any heresy whatever, not clarifying it (μὴ τρανώσας) even according to its intent (βούλημα), but heaping together the little words (ῥημάτια συμφορήσας), he displayed himself (ἐπεδείκνυτο) among those knowing nothing of ours or of those in the heresies as though he knew all the things of the Christians. The present passage (προκειμένη λέξις) makes this clear.
pass_b_english: After setting out what was mentioned above and things like it (the things we ourselves have added), Celsus says this: “And they go on adding one thing after another: words of prophets, and circles upon circles, and emanations of an earthly church and of circumcision, and the flowing power of a certain virgin, Prunicus, and a living soul, and a heaven slain that it may live, and an earth slain with a sword, and many slain that they may live, and death coming to an end in the world when the sin of the world dies, and again a narrow way down, and gates that open of their own accord. And there, everywhere, is the tree of life, and a resurrection of the flesh from a tree, because, I suppose, their teacher was nailed to a cross and was a carpenter by trade. So if he had happened to be thrown down a cliff, or pushed into a pit, or strangled with a noose, or if he had been a shoemaker or a stonecutter or a smith, there would be above the heavens a cliff of life, or a pit of resurrection, or a rope of immortality, or a blessed stone, or iron of love, or holy leather. Or what old woman, crooning a tale to lull a child to sleep, would not be ashamed to whisper such things?”

In this Celsus seems to me to be jumbling together things he has misheard. For it is likely that whenever he heard some scrap of a phrase from any heresy at all, he did not make it clear even according to that heresy’s own meaning, but piled up bits of words and showed off before people who know nothing either of our teachings or of those in the heresies, as though he really knew everything that belongs to the Christians. The passage before us makes this plain too.

choices.choice: Celsus’s words set in double quotation marks; Origen takes them apart phrase by phrase in 6.35-37. ‘After setting out ... (the things we ourselves have added)’: ἅτινα ἡμεῖς προσεθήκαμεν takes up τὰ ἀνάλογον αὐτοῖς and refers to the formulae Origen himself supplied in 6.31-33; the parenthesis keeps that clear. [ἐστιν] after σκῦτος ἅγιον is bracketed by the editor as an intrusion and is not translated. Προυνικοῦ τινος ... παρθένου rendered ‘a certain virgin, Prunicus’ (Prunicus is a Gnostic name of Wisdom; see 6.35). Allusions inside Celsus’s list (Genesis 2:9 tree of life; Genesis 2:7 ‘living soul’) are his garbled echoes and are taken up and cited where Origen discusses them (6.35-36), not here. The same ‘carpenter’ claim is answered at 6.36.
ἅτινα ἡμεῖς προσεθήκαμεν: '(the things we ourselves have added)', no added 'more'
πανταχοῦ δὲ ἐκεῖ: 'there, everywhere' (ἐκεῖ was dropped)

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; the English is from the Greek.
